Family Health

Bleeding between periods: causes, checks and when to get help

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Bleeding that happens between expected periods is called intermenstrual bleeding; light amounts are often described as spotting. It can have several explanations, many of them treatable. The timing and amount alone cannot identify the cause, so new or unexplained bleeding deserves a medical discussion even when it is only a little blood.

First decide how urgently you need help

Seek emergency care for very heavy bleeding with faintness, collapse, severe weakness, chest pain or trouble breathing. Severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain also needs urgent assessment. If pregnancy is possible, bleeding with one-sided pain, shoulder-tip pain or dizziness can indicate an ectopic pregnancy and should not wait for a routine appointment.

Contact a pregnancy-care service promptly about bleeding during a known pregnancy, including light spotting. Fever, significant pelvic pain, or feeling unwell with bleeding also warrants prompt advice. For stable, unexplained spotting without these symptoms, arrange an appointment with a primary-care clinician, gynecologist or sexual-health service. Any vaginal bleeding after menopause needs checking, even once.

A change in bleeding does not always mean a serious illness

A menstrual cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. Many adult cycles are roughly three to five weeks long, with bleeding over several days; age, contraception and your usual pattern affect what is expected. Bleeding between those periods is a symptom to discuss, not a diagnosis in itself.

Some people have a small amount of spotting around ovulation. Starting contraception can also produce expected changes. These possibilities make it inaccurate to say that every spot of blood means something dangerous. They also do not prove that a new episode is harmless, especially if it keeps happening, becomes heavier or comes with other symptoms.

Hormone changes and contraception

Estrogen and progesterone help coordinate the menstrual cycle and changes in the uterine lining. When ovulation is irregular or absent, bleeding may become irregular too. Thyroid problems and conditions affecting ovulation can contribute. Starting, stopping or missing hormonal contraceptive pills may also change the pattern.

Pills, patches, injections and implants can cause breakthrough bleeding, but they do not all follow the same timetable. With a hormonal intrauterine device, often called an IUS or hormonal IUD, spotting is common during the first three to six months and often decreases afterward. Implant-related irregular bleeding may persist rather than settling at three months.

A copper IUD contains no hormones and can make periods heavier or cause spotting. Tell your clinician which method you use, when it was started and whether use has been interrupted. New bleeding should not automatically be blamed on contraception: pregnancy, infection, medication interactions and other causes may still need consideration. You can discuss treatment or changing methods if the bleeding is troublesome.

Consider pregnancy as well as the calendar

A missed or unusually light period followed by spotting may need a pregnancy test. Bleeding can occur in an ongoing pregnancy, a miscarriage or an ectopic pregnancy. In an ectopic pregnancy, implantation occurs outside the main cavity of the uterus, most often in a fallopian tube.

Spotting does not by itself mean a miscarriage has occurred. Equally, the color of the blood or an app’s prediction cannot safely label it implantation bleeding or rule out an ectopic pregnancy. If pregnancy is possible and you have pain or feel unwell, seek assessment rather than waiting for the next expected period.

Fibroids, polyps and changes around the cervix

Fibroids are noncancerous growths in the muscle of the uterus. Depending on their location and size, they may affect bleeding. They can occur whether or not someone has given birth. Polyps are another type of growth that can occur in the uterus or on the cervix and may bleed.

Bleeding after sex can also come from vaginal dryness, irritation or changes to the surface of the cervix, such as cervical ectropion. These are different from a uterine hormone problem. An examination helps identify where blood is coming from and whether a growth or tissue change needs treatment.

Infection, inflammation and local irritation

An infection of the cervix or reproductive organs can cause unexpected bleeding. Some infections are sexually transmitted, including chlamydia; pelvic inflammatory disease, or PID, involves infection and inflammation higher in the reproductive tract. Pelvic pain or unusual discharge can occur, but an infection does not always cause obvious symptoms.

Sex itself is not an infection. Friction or dryness can cause contact bleeding, while infections acquired through sexual contact are a separate possibility. Avoid vaginal douching: it can disturb protective bacteria and increase the risk of infection. If a tampon or another object may have been left in the vagina, tell the clinician, particularly if there is odor, discharge or discomfort.

Other health conditions, medicines and less common causes

Significant weight changes, major changes in exercise or diet, and stress can accompany disrupted cycles. Thyroid disease and conditions such as diabetes may also be relevant to a broader assessment. None of these should be assumed to explain spotting without considering the rest of the history.

Medicines matter too. Blood thinners and aspirin can contribute to bleeding, and changes in hormonal treatment can alter its timing. Bring a list of prescriptions, nonprescription medicines and supplements rather than stopping something on your own.

Cancer is a less common explanation, but abnormal bleeding can occur with cancers of the cervix, uterine lining or vagina and, less commonly, ovarian cancer. This is one reason persistent bleeding and any bleeding after menopause should be assessed. Most spotting is not cancer; evaluation is how the possibilities are separated.

What to record before the appointment

Write down the start and end of your usual periods and the days of unexpected bleeding. Note whether it followed sex, how long it lasted, whether there were clots and how often a pad or other period product became soaked. Describe a change from your own normal pattern rather than trying to calculate an exact blood volume.

Include pain, fatigue, dizziness, fever, discharge, pregnancy possibility, recent treatment or procedures, and any medication changes. If you are not sure whether blood is vaginal or comes from urine or a bowel movement, say so. You do not need a perfect diary before asking for help, and urgent symptoms should not wait while you collect one.

Tests are chosen for the situation

A clinician will ask about your symptoms and medical history and may offer an abdominal, pelvic or vaginal examination. A speculum examination allows the vagina and cervix to be seen. Ask what each step is for, and tell the clinician if it is uncomfortable or you need a pause.

Initial tests may include a pregnancy test, a blood count to look for anemia when relevant, and testing for sexually transmitted infections. Thyroid or other blood tests are selected according to the history; a broad hormone panel is not automatically useful for every bleeding problem.

An ultrasound may help assess the uterus and ovaries. Some people need a closer examination of the cervix, a hysteroscopy to look inside the uterus, or a tissue sample from the cervix or uterine lining. A biopsy is not required for everyone. Age, persistence of bleeding, examination findings and risk factors guide whether it is appropriate.

Treatment depends on the cause

There is no single treatment for all bleeding between periods. Options might include treating an infection, adjusting contraception, managing an underlying condition or addressing a growth. Sometimes monitoring is appropriate after assessment. Discuss whether you want to become pregnant, because that can affect which treatments fit your situation.

Ibuprofen or naproxen can reduce menstrual cramps and, in selected cases, menstrual blood loss. They are not a default treatment for unexplained spotting. Check suitability with a clinician or pharmacist, especially if pregnancy is possible or you have a stomach ulcer, kidney disease, a bleeding disorder or take a blood thinner. Do not combine anti-inflammatory painkillers on your own.

Aspirin can increase bleeding, so do not add it as a remedy for this problem. If it was prescribed for another reason, contact the prescriber about the bleeding and follow your individual instructions rather than stopping it solely because of a general article.

Follow-up matters even if the bleeding stops

Some breakthrough bleeding settles on its own, but improvement does not always explain the original cause. Keep the agreed follow-up, particularly if spotting recurs or an examination or test was recommended. Untreated infection and other significant conditions can worsen, which is why persistent symptoms should not be ignored.

You cannot prevent every episode. Use contraception according to its instructions, ask for help with missed doses, and discuss side effects early. Balanced eating, sustainable activity and support with stress can benefit general health, but they do not replace investigation or guarantee regular periods. Ask what changes should prompt you to return and who will communicate any test results.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Hormones, contraception, infection, pregnancy-related problems and tissue changes can all affect bleeding. Symptoms alone do not establish one main cause.

Expected contraceptive bleeding differs by method. Persistent, new or troublesome bleeding may still need assessment.

How BeMama can help

Bring a short bleeding record and medication list. Ask what has been ruled out, what needs follow-up, and whether the plan fits your pregnancy intentions.

When to seek help

Emergency symptoms include heavy bleeding with collapse or marked weakness, and possible pregnancy with severe pain, shoulder pain or faintness. Seek prompt advice for bleeding in pregnancy and arrange assessment for unexplained or postmenopausal bleeding.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • New or unexplained spotting deserves a medical discussion.
  • Pregnancy possibility and accompanying symptoms determine urgency.
  • Different contraceptives produce different bleeding patterns.
  • A diary and medication list can make an assessment more useful.
  • Tests and treatment should fit the suspected cause.
  • Do not stop prescribed medicines or self-treat unexplained bleeding without advice.

Frequently asked questions

Is a hormone imbalance always the main cause?

No. Hormonal changes are one possibility, but contraception, pregnancy, infection, growths and other conditions can also cause bleeding.

Can ovulation cause a little spotting?

Yes, some people notice a small amount around ovulation. That timing alone does not establish the cause of new, persistent or painful bleeding.

Should contraceptive spotting stop within three months?

Not necessarily. The pattern depends on the method. Hormonal IUD spotting often settles over several months; implant-related changes may continue. Ask for advice if the pattern is new or bothersome.

Does spotting during pregnancy mean miscarriage?

Not always. Contact your pregnancy-care team for advice. Severe pain, faintness, shoulder pain or heavy bleeding need urgent assessment.

Can I ignore bleeding if it stops?

Some episodes settle, but unexplained or recurrent bleeding still needs discussion. Follow any recommended testing, and always have bleeding after menopause checked.

Will I need a biopsy?

Not everyone does. The clinician considers your age, symptoms, examination and risk factors before deciding whether tissue sampling or other tests are needed.

Can ibuprofen treat the cause?

It may help selected menstrual bleeding and cramps, but it does not diagnose or treat every cause of spotting. Check whether it is suitable for you, especially if pregnancy is possible or other medicines are involved.

Should I stop my prescribed aspirin?

Ask the prescriber promptly and follow your personal instructions. A general warning that aspirin can increase bleeding should not replace the reason it was prescribed.

Can exercise or a healthier diet prevent it?

They can support general health, but they cannot prevent every cause. Persistent symptoms need assessment rather than lifestyle changes alone.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
